solution:
Count the electrons that oxygen keeps to itself in each structure.

In structure (A) the oxygen is neutral and doubly bonded. A neutral oxygen atom has 6 valence electrons; two of them are used in the two shared pairs of the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) bond, so 4 electrons remain as 2 unshared (lone) pairs. Unshared electrons on oxygen in (A) \(= 4\).

In structure (B) the oxygen carries a negative charge and only a single bond. The negatively charged oxygen has \(6 + 1 = 7\) valence electrons; one of them is used in the single \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond, leaving 6 electrons as 3 unshared pairs. Unshared electrons on oxygen in (B) \(= 6\).

So the pair is 4, 6 in the order (A), (B).

Why the other three fail: "2, 4" and "2, 6" both put only one lone pair (2 electrons) on the oxygen of (A), which would leave that oxygen with just 6 electrons in its valence shell — an incomplete octet, which the drawn structure does not show. "6, 4" is the correct pair of numbers written in the wrong order: the three lone pairs belong to the singly bonded, negatively charged oxygen — the one drawn in the SECOND structure — while the doubly bonded oxygen of the first structure keeps only two lone pairs.

Section 12.8.3 of the chapter describes Wolf-Kishner reduction as treatment of the carbonyl compound with hydrazine, followed by heating with sodium or potassium hydroxide in a high boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol. The first of those two operations is a reaction between the carbonyl group and hydrazine \((\mathrm{NH_2-NH_2})\), and Table 12.7 of the same chapter names the product of that reaction: an aldehyde or ketone plus hydrazine loses water to give \(\mathrm{R'(R)C=N-NH_2}\), a hydrazone.

\(\mathrm{Ar-CO-R} + \mathrm{NH_2-NH_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ar(R)C=N-NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The hydrazone is then heated with \(\mathrm{KOH}\) in ethylene glycol, when it loses nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen ends up replaced by two hydrogen atoms, giving the alkyl benzene.

Why the other three fail: acids would require the ketone to be oxidised, whereas this sequence is a reduction; alcohols are what a hydride reducing agent such as \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) or \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\) would give, and no alcohol appears anywhere in the Wolf-Kishner sequence; alkenes are never formed, because the carbonyl carbon ends up as a saturated \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) group.

Aldol condensation happens in two stages. In the first, the carbanion (enolate) generated from the \(\alpha\)-carbon of one molecule attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second molecule; nothing leaves that carbon, so this stage is a nucleophilic ADDITION and its product is the \(\beta\)-hydroxy carbonyl compound (the aldol). In the second stage the aldol is warmed and loses a molecule of water across the \(\alpha\),\(\beta\)-positions — an ELIMINATION — giving the \(\alpha\),\(\beta\)-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

\(2\ \mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CHO}\)

The chapter states the classification in exactly these terms in section 12.8.2 (g): the overall reaction is called aldol condensation and it is a nucleophilic addition-elimination reaction.

Why the other three fail: nothing attacks the substrate as an electrophile, so it is not an electrophilic substitution; no group is displaced from a carbon atom by an incoming nucleophile, so it is not a nucleophilic substitution; and naming it an elimination reaction describes only the dehydration half and leaves out the carbon-carbon bond-forming addition step that makes the aldol in the first place.

The acidity of a substituted benzoic acid is decided by what the substituent does to the negative charge of the carboxylate conjugate base. An electron-withdrawing group disperses that charge and stabilises the anion, so the acid becomes stronger; an electron-donating group intensifies the charge and destabilises the anion, so the acid becomes weaker. The chapter states this directly: electron-withdrawing groups like \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), \(\mathrm{-CN}\) and \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) increase the acidity of substituted benzoic acids, while electron-donating groups like \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) decrease it.

Taking benzoic acid (\(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}\) 4.2 in the chapter) as the reference:

- \(\mathrm{3-NO_2-C_6H_4-COOH}\) carries a nitro group, strongly electron-withdrawing — MORE acidic than benzoic acid.
- \(\mathrm{2-Cl-C_6H_4-COOH}\) carries a chlorine, electron-withdrawing by \(-\mathrm{I}\) and close to the carboxyl group — MORE acidic than benzoic acid.
- \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-COOH}\) is the unsubstituted reference itself.
- \(\mathrm{4-OCH_3-C_6H_4-COOH}\) carries a methoxy group, which the chapter lists as electron-donating — LESS acidic than benzoic acid.

Only the methoxy compound falls below benzoic acid, so it has the lowest acidity of the four.

Section 12.9.7 of the chapter (Reduction of carboxylic acids) says that a carboxylic acid can be reduced to a primary alcohol by diborane, and adds the selectivity in the same sentence: diborane does not reduce \(\mathrm{-COOR}\), \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) or \(\mathrm{-X}\).

\(\mathrm{R-COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} \mathrm{R-CH_2OH}\)

That single statement eliminates the other three options one for one: \(\mathrm{-COOR}\) is the ester group, \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) the nitro group and \(\mathrm{-X}\) the halo group, and diborane leaves all three untouched. The functional group it does reduce is the carboxyl (acid) group.

Benzaldehyde is an aromatic aldehyde, so it responds to the tests that detect the \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group by mild oxidation or by addition:

- Schiff reagent gives the pink/magenta colour with an aldehyde, so benzaldehyde is positive.
- Tollens' reagent oxidises an aldehyde to the carboxylate ion and deposits a silver mirror; benzaldehyde gives this test, and the chapter itself shows benzaldehyde reacting under Tollens'-type conditions.
- Sodium bisulphite adds across the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones to give a crystalline bisulphite adduct (section 12.8.2 b), so benzaldehyde is positive here too.

Fehling solution, however, is a much milder oxidising agent and aromatic aldehydes do not reduce it — no red precipitate of cuprous oxide is formed. The chapter poses this very fact as a "Use your brain power" question on the page dealing with the laboratory tests: Why is benzaldehyde NOT oxidized by Fehling solution ? So the test benzaldehyde fails is the one with Fehling solution.
